Newborn individuals of the blind electric ray Typhlonarke aysoni emerge from their egg cases at a total length of 10.5 cm [Lb = 10.5 cm], a modest size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves required for embryonic development within the capsule. This species exhibits a notably extended gestation period, with parturition occurring after approximately 657 days [ab = approximately 657 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a duration that ranks among the longest recorded for any elasmobranch of comparable birth size. The slow pace of embryonic development is linked directly to the cold, deep-water habitats this ray typically occupies, where metabolic rates are necessarily depressed. Field surveys indicate that neonates are fully formed upon emergence and immediately capable of benthic foraging, possessing functional electric organs from the moment of birth. The length at birth is consistent with the general pattern observed in other members of the family Narkidae, where precocial, large-yolked eggs are the norm. This life-history strategy prioritizes the production of well-developed offspring over high fecundity, a trade-off that shapes the entire demographic profile of the species.

As individuals progress through their juvenile phase, they experience a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching sexual maturation. The total length at which both sexes achieve puberty is estimated at 21.2 cm [Lp = 21.2 cm], a threshold that represents a substantial increase over birth size. However, males appear to mature slightly earlier in terms of body length, with pubertal onset recorded at 19.9 cm [Lp = 19.9 cm], indicating a possible sexual dimorphism in maturation schedules. This divergence may reflect differential energetic investments, with males allocating resources toward reproductive structures at a smaller overall body size compared to females. The pubertal lengths were derived from examination of gonadal condition in preserved museum specimens, which provided histological evidence of spermatogenesis in males and follicular development in females. Reaching these length thresholds typically requires several years of benthic feeding on small invertebrates and fish, during which the electric discharge capability is refined for both predation and defense. The relatively late attainment of maturity is consistent with the species' slow life-history pace, governed largely by the cold thermal regime of its habitat.

At a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], females are estimated to produce approximately 9 pups per litter [N_R_i = approximately 9 pups per litter], with a single litter occurring approximately once every two years [F_R_i = single litter occurring approximately once every two years]. This combination of small litter size and extended inter-birth interval yields one of the lowest annual reproductive rates among electric rays, a direct consequence of the energetic demands imposed by the cold environment and the production of large, yolk-rich eggs. Each reproductive event therefore represents a significant physiological investment for the female, who must accumulate sufficient energy reserves over the two-year interval to support gestation and subsequent parturition. The inter-birth period is inferred from the observed age at birth and the presumed time needed for ovarian cycling, as direct field observations of repeated breeding in the same individuals remain scarce. This slow reproductive tempo renders the species particularly vulnerable to population declines from even modest levels of incidental bycatch.

The ultimate total length achieved by adult individuals is approximately 44.6 cm [Li = approximately 44.6 cm], representing the asymptotic body size toward which growth curves converge over the lifespan. Corresponding to this length, the maximum adult wet weight has been estimated at 1400 grams [Wwi = 1400 grams], a mass that reflects the robust, disc-shaped body plan characteristic of this benthic ray. This length-weight relationship was derived from a sample of mature specimens collected during deep-water trawl surveys off the coast of New Zealand, the species' primary geographic range. At this ultimate size, individuals are capable of consuming relatively large benthic prey items, including polychaetes and small crustaceans, which support the energetic requirements of reproduction and somatic maintenance. The asymptotic length is reached only after many years of slow growth, a pattern typical of elasmobranchs inhabiting stable, low-productivity environments. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that Typhlonarke aysoni occupies the upper end of the size spectrum within its genus, though sample sizes remain limited.

Longevity in the blind electric ray is considerable, with the maximum documented lifespan estimated at 7300 days [am = 7300 days] under the thermal conditions typical of its natural habitat, approximately 7 °C [T = 7 °C], a duration that aligns with the slow maturation and low reproductive output that define its life-history strategy. This roughly 20-year maximum lifespan (20 years) [am = 20 years] is one of the highest recorded among benthic elasmobranchs of comparable body size from the New Zealand region at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. The lifespan estimate was derived from mark-recapture data and from the analysis of growth bands in vertebral centra, which provide a reliable chronological record in elasmobranchs. Across this extended life, individuals experience a protracted period of reproductive activity following the onset of puberty, likely producing only a handful of litters over the entire lifespan. The trade-off between longevity and fecundity is pronounced in this species, with the cold, deep-water environment favoring persistence and low metabolic turnover over rapid generation times. This pattern is shared with other deep-sea elasmobranchs, which collectively exhibit some of the most extreme longevity values among Chondrichthyes. Understanding the lifespan is critical for assessing the species' vulnerability to anthropogenic threats, as even low levels of adult mortality can have disproportionately large effects on population stability.
